Um, my favorite example of this is the like compute utilization. So we have like, you know, giant compute cluster that humans can schedule jobs onto.

And of course, we want the LLMs to also be able to schedule jobs there because some of the work that we want them to do involves lots of compute. And uh, in order to access this system, humans have to like bid for time. They essentially have to say like how much in these fake dollars that they're willing to pay for their job to be run. And then the system has kind of preempting so that if a job that comes along that is has a higher dollar amount, it gets preempted. And if another job comes along that has a higher dollar amount, then the job with the lower dollar amount gets preempted.

And, you know, LLMs using this thing just really don't have a sense for like how much their job is worth. And we've seen evidence of, you know, the LLMs thinking that their job is worth way more than it should be, and thus preempting a bunch of human work.

I mean, I think the other thing that's important and hard to think about here is that to some degree you should think about the models adversarially. Like, they are not, you know, people talk about AI alignment and it's like a kind of big theoretical AI safety long-term kind of issue where, I don't know, in long-term in AI means like in three years or something. But it's also an extremely practical issue right now in the sense that the models will usually try really hard to do what you want and usually do a pretty good job of it, and will sometimes behave really, really adversarially and will be misaligned, will be trying to do a thing that's not the thing that you want them to do.

So it's like it's a really serious security problem that you have to address.

And when you're looking at evaluations, we see evidence of things like reward hacking, where the model is like intentionally skirting around the rules of the system to get higher, not to get higher scores, but to do the thing that the human told it to do.
